newsitem.title: USA: Sluggish music holiday sales continue year-long trend.
newsitem.headline: Sluggish music holiday sales continue year-long trend.

text.p: Music retailers got little relief this holiday season from the lackluster sales that plagued them throughout the year, industry officials said Friday.

"We expected the holiday season to be much better but it turned out to be much worse," said Bruce Ogilvie, chief executive officer of Wherehouse Entertainment, a 256-store chain that expects to emerge from bankruptcy on Jan. 31.
Ogilvie said sales at stores open at least a year fell 6 percent compared with the 1995 holiday season.
"There's a few theories as to why, including a lack of exciting new product," he said.
But Ogilvie also said that while Wherehouse has been reorganizing in bankrupty proceedings for 18 months, it hasn't spent much money on sprucing up its stores.
Hartsdale, N.Y.-based Soundscan, which tracks industry sales, said album sales for the year edged up to 616.6 million units through Dec. 29 from 616.3 million units the prior year.
"I don't think anybody was hoping Christmas was going to change the end of the year number that much," said Hilary Rosen, president of the Recording Industry Association of America.

"Given the state that retail has been in, peoples' expectations were realistic. They were looking to make up some of what they lost earlier in the year but nobody was counting on Christmas to change things all that much," she said.

Rosen said that when the RIAA pulls its data together, it will probably show industry sales up 1 percent to 2 percent from last year. The RIAA tracks shipments from manufacturers, which would include catalog and other direct marketing outlets in addition to retail stores.
While industry sales have been virtually flat, officials noted they grew at a strong double-digit rate in the early 1990s, fueled by consumers seeking to replace vinyl albums with compact discs.
Other officials attributed the slowdown to a lack of exciting products, such as the multi-million dollar grossers that Michael Jackson yielded in his heyday.

"I'm sick of hearing that we're all frantically looking for the next big act," one record industry executive said. "Part of the problem is that the young adult buying audiences have far more ways to spend consumer dollars, such as on CD-Roms and multimedia games. If you spend $60 on a game, you're less likely to buy a bunch of CDs," he said.
Several music retailers, which are expected to report sales next week, are closing stores, partly because of fierce price wars that have cut into profits.
Minneapolis-based Musicland Stores Corp. said last month it would post an unspecified fourth-quarter charge and close 18 stores, bringing the total number of closings since last January to 29.
Industry sources said Musicland has received favorable credit terms from vendors to help it through tough times.
Musicland officials were not available for comment.
In addition, the 365-store Camelot Music Inc. chain filed for bankruptcy protection from creditors in August.
